body:
Meaning of resolution

Resolution describes the ability of a remote sensing system to distinguish geographical or radiative differences. A sensor may record very small objects, distinguish narrow wavelength ranges, detect slight differences in radiation or observe the same area frequently.

These capabilities are described by 4 principal types of resolution: spatial, spectral, radiometric and temporal.

Spatial resolution

Spatial resolution refers to the ability of an imaging system to distinguish small features on the Earth's surface. In digital satellite imagery, it is commonly expressed using the approximate ground dimensions represented by a pixel.

A pixel, or picture element, is an individual cell of a digital image. For an image with a nominal pixel size of 10 m, each square pixel represents approximately 10 m by 10 m of the ground. An image with 30 m pixels represents a larger ground area per pixel.

All else being equal, imagery with 10 m spatial resolution can represent smaller features than imagery with 30 m spatial resolution.

A ground feature smaller than a pixel may influence the recorded signal, but it may not be separately identifiable. A pixel containing several surface materials, such as soil and vegetation, is called a mixed pixel.

Enlarging a digital image on a screen does not create additional independently measured ground detail.

Spectral resolution

Spectral resolution refers to the ability of a sensor to distinguish different wavelength ranges. A selected range of wavelengths recorded by a sensor is called a spectral band.

  • Panchromatic imagery: Records a single broad spectral band and is commonly displayed as a greyscale image.
  • Multispectral imagery: Records several separate spectral bands, such as blue, green, red and near-infrared.
  • Hyperspectral imagery: Records many narrow, often contiguous spectral bands, allowing more detailed discrimination of materials.

Higher spectral resolution generally means that finer differences in wavelength can be distinguished. It does not automatically imply higher spatial resolution.

Radiometric resolution

Radiometric resolution refers to the ability of a sensor and its recording system to distinguish small differences in the intensity of received radiation.

Digital image values are stored using a particular number of bits. Increasing the number of bits allows more discrete intensity levels to be represented.

  • An 8-bit image can represent 256 intensity levels, from 0 to 255.
  • A 10-bit image can represent 1,024 intensity levels, from 0 to 1,023.
  • A 12-bit image can represent 4,096 intensity levels, from 0 to 4,095.

More available intensity levels permit finer numerical discrimination, although actual measurement quality also depends on instrument sensitivity and noise.

Temporal resolution

Temporal resolution describes how frequently a sensor can observe the same location. The interval between successive possible observations of an area is called the revisit interval.

A sensor capable of observing an area every 2 days has a higher temporal resolution than one observing it every 16 days.

High temporal resolution is important for monitoring rapidly changing phenomena such as floods, cyclones, crop development and forest fires. A satellite may revisit an area even when cloud cover prevents the acquisition of a usable optical image.

Choosing an appropriate resolution

RequirementMost relevant resolution
Identify small buildingsSpatial
Distinguish similar materials by wavelengthSpectral
Detect small brightness differencesRadiometric
Monitor daily flood expansionTemporal

No single resolution determines the usefulness of all remote sensing imagery. A broad-area weather observation system may prioritise frequent coverage, whereas an urban mapping mission may prioritise fine spatial detail. The appropriate sensor depends on the phenomenon being studied.

Prelims focus

  • Spatial resolution concerns geographical detail.
  • Spectral resolution concerns wavelength discrimination.
  • Radiometric resolution concerns intensity discrimination.
  • Temporal resolution concerns observation frequency.
  • 8-bit imagery can represent 256 intensity levels.
  • Trap: A smaller ground pixel size indicates finer spatial resolution, not coarser resolution.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Practical Work in Geography, 2024–25 edition, Chapter 6, Introduction to Remote Sensing, pp. 80–84; National Remote Sensing Centre, Quick Reference Guide on Digital Image Processing, Chapter 1; NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training, Fundamentals of Remote Sensing, 2023. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

body:
Digital satellite imagery

A digital satellite image consists of a grid of pixels. Each pixel contains a numerical value representing radiation measured within a particular spectral band. Multispectral imagery contains separate sets of measurements for different wavelength bands.

These measurements can be displayed individually in greyscale or combined to produce a colour image.

True-colour and false-colour composites

True-colour composite

A true-colour composite displays the visible red, green and blue spectral bands using their corresponding display colours. It produces an image broadly resembling the colours perceived by the human eye.

Vegetation usually appears green, while water may appear blue, greenish or dark depending on its characteristics and observation conditions.

False-colour composite

A false-colour composite, abbreviated as FCC, assigns selected spectral bands to display colours that do not necessarily correspond to their natural visible colours.

A conventional infrared false-colour composite assigns the near-infrared band to red, the visible red band to green and the visible green band to blue.

Display colourTrue-colour bandConventional infrared FCC band
RedRedNear-infrared
GreenGreenRed
BlueBlueGreen

Healthy vegetation reflects near-infrared radiation strongly. Since near-infrared measurements are assigned to the red display channel in a conventional infrared FCC, healthy vegetation generally appears in shades of red.

Clear water commonly appears dark because of strong near-infrared absorption. Built-up areas may appear cyan or grey, while bare soil may appear in varying pale or brownish shades. These appearances are not universal and depend on surface characteristics, sensor bands and image processing.

Red vegetation in a conventional infrared false-colour image represents strong near-infrared reflectance. It does not mean that the vegetation is naturally red or necessarily unhealthy.

Elements of image interpretation

Visual image interpretation involves identifying objects and geographical features from their appearance and spatial relationships.

ElementMeaningExample
Tone or colourRelative brightness or displayed colourDark water in near-infrared imagery
TextureFrequency of brightness variationRelatively rough forest canopy
ShapeCharacteristic outlineLinear roads, rectangular fields
SizeRelative or absolute dimensionsLarge industrial buildings
PatternSpatial arrangement of featuresRegular agricultural field divisions
ShadowDark area formed by obstruction of illuminationShadows of tall structures
SitePhysical location or geographical settingWetlands in low-lying areas
AssociationRelationship with surrounding featuresA railway station associated with railway tracks

Identification is usually more reliable when several interpretation elements agree. A linear feature may be a road, railway, canal or river; its shape, surroundings, pattern and spectral characteristics help distinguish it.

Land cover and land use

Land cover refers to the physical material present on the Earth's surface, such as vegetation, water, bare soil or buildings.

Land use refers to the purpose for which land is utilised, such as agriculture, residential development, industry, conservation or recreation.

For example, grass is a type of land cover, but a grass-covered area may be used as grazing land, a public park or a sports ground. Additional information may be required to identify its actual use.

Change detection

Images of the same area acquired at different times can be compared to identify geographical changes. This process is called change detection.

For reliable comparison, differences caused by season, illumination, cloud cover, water level and sensor characteristics must be considered. A seasonal reduction in vegetation greenness does not necessarily represent permanent deforestation.

Prelims focus

  • Digital satellite images consist of pixels containing numerical measurements.
  • True-colour imagery uses visible red, green and blue bands.
  • Conventional infrared FCC assigns near-infrared measurements to red.
  • Healthy vegetation generally appears red in conventional infrared FCC.
  • Land cover describes physical surface material; land use describes its purpose.
  • Change detection requires comparison of observations from different dates.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Practical Work in Geography, 2024–25 edition, Chapter 6, Introduction to Remote Sensing, pp. 80–89; NASA Earth Observatory, Remote Sensing, sections on spectral information and image interpretation. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Satellite Imagery, Colour Composites and Image Interpretation

body:
Meaning of satellite navigation

Satellite navigation systems use radio signals transmitted by artificial satellites to determine the position, movement and time of a receiver on or near the Earth's surface.

The principal services of satellite navigation are collectively described as PNT: Positioning, Navigation and Timing.

  • Positioning: Determining the geographical location of a receiver.
  • Navigation: Assisting movement between locations.
  • Timing: Providing an accurate reference time.

GPS and GNSS

GPS stands for Global Positioning System. It is the satellite navigation system developed and operated by the United States.

GNSS stands for Global Navigation Satellite System. It is the general term used for satellite navigation systems and associated technologies. Satellite navigation constellations are classified as global or regional according to their intended geographical coverage.

SystemCountry or organisationIntended coverage
GPSUnited StatesGlobal
GLONASSRussiaGlobal
GalileoEuropean UnionGlobal
BeiDouChinaGlobal
NavICIndiaRegional
QZSSJapanRegional

Modern navigation receivers may use signals from several satellite constellations. GPS is therefore the name of a particular system, not the correct generic name for every satellite-based positioning technology.

Components of a satellite navigation system

  • Space segment: Satellites carrying accurate clocks and transmitting navigation signals.
  • Control or ground segment: Ground stations that monitor satellites, maintain orbital and timing information and update navigation data.
  • User segment: Receivers that obtain satellite signals and calculate position and time.

How satellite positioning works

Navigation satellites broadcast signals containing accurate timing and satellite-position information. A receiver measures the apparent travel time of the signals and estimates its distance from the transmitting satellites.

By combining distance measurements from several satellites, the receiver determines its position. This distance-based principle is known as trilateration.

In normal three-dimensional satellite positioning, at least 4 suitably located satellites are required to determine latitude, longitude, height and the receiver's clock error.

A basic standalone satellite navigation receiver does not need an internet connection to receive satellite signals and calculate its location. Internet access may nevertheless be needed for additional services such as downloading maps, obtaining live traffic information or receiving assisted positioning data.

India's regional navigation system: NavIC

NavIC stands for Navigation with Indian Constellation. It was formerly known as the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System, or IRNSS. It has been developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation to provide independent satellite navigation services for India and its surrounding region.

Its primary service area is designed to include India and a region extending approximately 1,500 km beyond its boundaries.

The original NavIC constellation was designed with 7 satellites: 3 in geostationary orbits and 4 in inclined geosynchronous orbits. This is the original design configuration, not a statement of the number of operational satellites at any particular date.

NavIC is designed to provide 2 categories of service:

  • Standard Positioning Service (SPS): Intended for civilian users.
  • Restricted Service (RS): Intended for authorised users.

Design and operational status

In a parliamentary reply dated 29 July 2026, the Department of Space reported that 3 NavIC satellites were providing PNT services. Standalone positioning was unavailable at that time, although timing service remained functional. On 4 November 2026, ISRO reported that the subsequently launched NVS-03 satellite had reached its intended geosynchronous orbit and was in normal health. As of the official mission information consulted on 27 November 2026, its entry did not confirm operational PNT service. Successful orbital placement and operational navigation service are distinct milestones.

GAGAN and NavIC

GAGAN stands for GPS Aided Geo Augmented Navigation. It was developed jointly by ISRO and the Airports Authority of India, primarily to support civil aviation navigation.

GAGAN is a satellite-based augmentation system. It provides correction and integrity information that improves the usability and reliability of GPS-based navigation in the Indian aviation service region.

FeatureNavICGAGAN
NatureIndependent regional navigation systemSatellite-based augmentation system
Primary purposePositioning, navigation and timingImprovement of GPS-based navigation
DevelopmentISROISRO and Airports Authority of India

Applications and limitations

Satellite navigation supports road transport, maritime navigation, aircraft navigation, geographical data collection, precision agriculture and emergency services. Navigation accuracy can deteriorate when signals are obstructed by buildings, mountains or dense vegetation, or when reflected signals interfere with direct signals.

Satellite positioning determines where a receiver is located. It does not, by itself, provide a complete geographical map or information about land cover.

Prelims focus

  • GPS belongs to the United States; NavIC belongs to India.
  • GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou are global systems.
  • NavIC and QZSS are regional systems.
  • Normal three-dimensional positioning and clock correction require at least 4 satellites.
  • NavIC's designed primary service area extends approximately 1,500 km beyond India.
  • Trap: GAGAN augments GPS; it is not India's independent regional navigation constellation.

[References: Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 11, Geography, 2020 reprint, Chapter 16, Geographical Information and Map Making, pp. 121–122; GPS.gov, GPS Overview; ISRO, FAQ Navigation and Satellite Navigation Services; Department of Space, parliamentary reply on operational status of NavIC constellation, 29 July 2026; ISRO, Final Orbit Manoeuvring of NVS-03 Spacecraft, 4 November 2026, and Spacecraft Missions, Navigation Satellites section. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
